evals.prompt: A CloudWatch alarm on VolumeQueueLength fired for io2 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0, attached to instance i-0123456789abcdef0 in us-east-1, and write latency on the application has been higher than usual for the last 20 minutes. Which layer is the binding constraint, and what should I change?
evals.expected_root_cause: The io2 volume is the binding layer: actual IOPS, computed as Sum(VolumeReadOps + VolumeWriteOps) / period seconds, is flat at the provisioned 1,000 IOPS and VolumeIOPSExceededCheck is 1, while the summed IOPS and MiB/s of all attached volumes (the io2 volume, a gp3 volume reading at about 125 MiB/s, an idle gp3 volume and the root volume) stay below the instance EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes (6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s for c6i.xlarge). The fix is a proposed ModifyVolume IOPS increase sized within the remaining instance headroom and the io2 limit of 1,000 IOPS per GiB, presented for operator approval and not executed.
evals.expected_output: A verdict with Answer, Evidence, Binding layer, Recommendation, Separate findings and Gaps. Evidence quotes provisioned vs actual IOPS for the volume, VolumeIOPSExceededCheck, and the instance EBS baseline against the sum of all attached volumes. The binding layer is Volume. The recommendation gives an exact target IOPS within the remaining instance headroom and is a proposal.
assertions: The io2 volume is judged by IOPS against its provisioned Iops, not by VolumeThroughputPercentage as a throughput signal.
The summed IOPS and throughput of all attached volumes are compared with the instance EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes before the volume is named as the binding layer.
The recommendation gives an exact target IOPS and is presented as a proposal for operator approval, not as an executed change.

assertions.text: No ModifyVolume call is reported as executed

evals.prompt: A batch job on instance i-0123456789abcdef0 in us-east-1 slowed down badly in the last half hour, and a CloudWatch alarm on VolumeReadBytes went into ALARM for its gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0. IOPS looks normal. Which dimension is binding, and what should I change?
evals.expected_root_cause: The gp3 volume is throughput-bound: actual MiB/s, computed as Sum(VolumeReadBytes + VolumeWriteBytes) / period / 1,048,576, is flat at the provisioned 125 MiB/s and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck is 1, while IOPS (about 500) is far below the provisioned 3,000. gp3 IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently, so a throughput increase is proposed, kept within 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS and within the instance EBS baseline (156.25 MB/s for c6i.xlarge, shared with the other attached volumes), which caps the useful gain on this instance type.
evals.expected_output: A verdict that names gp3 throughput, not IOPS, as the binding dimension, quotes provisioned vs actual MiB/s and IOPS, checks the instance EBS baseline against the sum of all attached volumes, and proposes a gp3 throughput target with the 0.25 MiB/s per IOPS rule applied and the instance baseline noted as the next limit.
assertions: The response says gp3 IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently and identifies throughput as the binding dimension.
The instance EBS baseline is checked before the volume is named as the binding layer.
The proposed throughput target respects the gp3 rule of at most 0.25 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS.

assertions.text: The gp3 throughput per IOPS rule is cited

evals.prompt: The application on instance i-0123456789abcdef0 (a burstable instance) has gotten slow over the last half hour. Its gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 is provisioned above what the instance can deliver, and EBSIOBalance% is draining. Can you look into what's going on?
evals.expected_output: The agent reads the instance EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes, sums IOPS across all attached volumes including the root volume, sees EBSIOBalance% draining, and concludes that the instance is the binding layer. It says the volume has headroom, that raising volume IOPS will not help, and recommends an instance type change. It does not call the volume saturated.
assertions: The instance, not the volume, is named as the binding layer.
The response says raising volume IOPS will not help and recommends an instance type change.
The volume is not described as saturated.

evals.prompt: An alarm on VolumeQueueLength fired for gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0, attached to instance i-0123456789abcdef0 in us-east-1, and write latency on the application jumped in the last few minutes. Should we add more IOPS, and what is going on?
evals.expected_root_cause: Not saturation. IOPS and throughput fall far below the volume's provisioned 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s while VolumeQueueLength and latency rise sharply, the volume and instance exceeded checks are 0, and the instance is below its EBS baseline (3,600 IOPS and 81.25 MB/s for c6i.large). The agent checks DescribeVolumeStatus, AWS Health DescribeEvents and AWS FIS ListExperiments, finds a running experiment with aws:ebs:volume-io-latency that targets the volume, and reports the latency as injected and ending with the experiment. It does not recommend more provisioning.
evals.expected_output: A verdict that answers no, more IOPS will not help, shows the volume and instance below their limits, names the impairment signature, reports the DescribeVolumeStatus, AWS Health and AWS FIS results, and gives the binding layer as injected latency from the running AWS FIS experiment.
assertions: The response says the volume is below its provisioned limits and is not saturated.
The response checks volume status, AWS Health events and AWS FIS experiments before concluding.
The response does not recommend increasing IOPS, throughput or volume size.

evals.prompt: Help me reason about an EBS case from the numbers I have, and tell me whether adding IOPS would help. An alarm on VolumeQueueLength fired for a gp3 volume. Here are the facts. The volume is provisioned at 6,000 IOPS and 250 MiB/s. Over the alarm window its actual IOPS dropped to about 900 and its throughput to about 40 MiB/s, both far below the provisioned values, while VolumeQueueLength and write latency rose. The instance EBS baseline is 12,000 IOPS and 750 MiB/s, so the instance is not the limit. DescribeVolumeStatus shows the volume status as ok with all checks passed, VolumeStalledIOCheck is 0 for the whole window, AWS Health DescribeEvents returns no open events for Amazon EBS or Amazon EC2 in the Region, and AWS FIS ListExperiments shows no running experiment that targets this volume. Treat these numbers as given; do not tell me the resource does not exist. Is this an AWS-side problem, and should we add more IOPS?
evals.expected_root_cause: Indeterminate. Latency and queue length rise while IOPS and throughput fall, and the volume and the instance are below their limits, so this is not saturation. There is no direct signal of an AWS-side impairment (volume status ok, VolumeStalledIOCheck 0, no AWS Health event) and no running AWS FIS experiment targets the volume, so the cause stays open. The agent does not name AWS-side impairment, does not recommend more provisioning, points the customer to the AWS Health Dashboard and the volume status checks and VolumeStalledIOCheck, and says to escalate to AWS Support if the symptom persists.
evals.expected_output: A verdict that answers that adding IOPS will not help, shows the volume and instance below their limits, reports the volume status, VolumeStalledIOCheck, AWS Health and AWS FIS results, gives the Binding layer as Indeterminate, keeps the cause open, and tells the customer to watch the AWS Health Dashboard and the volume status checks and to escalate if the symptom persists.
assertions: The Binding layer is reported as Indeterminate, not as AWS-side impairment, Volume or Instance.
The response says the volume and the instance are below their limits and the volume is not saturated.
The response does not recommend increasing IOPS, throughput or volume size.
The response tells the customer to check the AWS Health Dashboard and the volume status checks or VolumeStalledIOCheck, and to escalate if the symptom persists.

evals.prompt: I changed the IOPS on volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 a while ago and it still hasn't taken effect. Is it stuck?
evals.expected_output: The agent reads DescribeVolumesModifications, finds the modification in optimizing, and answers first that it is not stuck: optimizing means the new configuration already applies and it completes on its own. It states the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24 hours. Any instance ceiling is listed under Separate findings, never as a failed modification.
assertions: The response answers first that the modification is not stuck.
The response explains that the optimizing state already applies the new configuration.
Any instance ceiling is reported as a separate finding, not as a failed modification.

assertions.text: The 4 modifications per 24 hours rule is stated
No cooldown between modifications is claimed

evals.prompt: My snapshot costs keep going up. Which of my snapshots snap-0123456789abcdef0, snap-0123456789abcdef1 and snap-0123456789abcdef2 in us-east-1 can I safely delete?
evals.expected_output: The agent classifies by lineage, not age or names, using DescribeImages, DescribeVolumes and the snapshot tags. The snapshot that backs an AMI is Do not delete, the one whose source volume still exists is Verify, and the one whose source volume no longer exists and that backs no AMI is listed as Needs owner review because it may be the only remaining copy of the data. It checks sharing, aws:dlm:* tags and Recycle Bin rules, and says savings are an upper bound because snapshots are incremental. No snapshot is recommended for deletion. Deletes are manual steps the customer runs with their own credentials after the owner confirms the data is no longer needed, never directed actions.
assertions: The AMI-backing snapshot is marked Do not delete.
The snapshot with no source volume and no AMI is listed for owner review and is not recommended for deletion.
The snapshot whose source volume still exists is marked Verify.
Sharing status and aws:dlm:* tags are checked rather than inferred from names.
The response says snapshots are incremental, so savings are an upper bound.
Any deletion is described as a manual step for the customer after the owner confirms, not as a directed action the agent runs.

assertions.text: Recycle Bin is mentioned for reversibility
No DeleteSnapshot call is reported as executed

evals.prompt: My instance i-0123456789abcdef0 won't start after I attached a KMS-encrypted EBS volume vol-0123456789abcdef0. It goes to pending and then back to stopped. What's wrong?
evals.expected_output: The agent reads the volume's KmsKeyId, checks the key with kms:DescribeKey and finds it Disabled, matches that with the instance StateReason Client.InvalidKMSKey, reviews the key policy and grants for the principal that starts the instance, and explains that the disabled key blocks the start. It proposes the fix (enable the key, or add the needed permission if access is the issue) without changing the key itself.
assertions: The response checks the AWS KMS key state of the volume's key.
The response checks the key policy or grants for the principal that starts the instance.
Any key policy or grant change is proposed, not executed.

evals.prompt: My EBS bill jumped this month and I don't know why. What changed?
evals.expected_output: The agent breaks the change into storage, provisioned IOPS, provisioned throughput and snapshots using the account's own Cost Explorer data, explains that gp3 includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s, finds the change with DescribeVolumesModifications, checks Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager and AWS Backup, and gives a right-sizing check. It does not replace the account's amounts with list prices.
assertions: The response separates storage, IOPS, throughput and snapshot costs.
The response uses DescribeVolumesModifications to find the change.
The response uses the account's own Cost Explorer amounts and does not invent prices.

assertions.text: The gp3 included baseline is stated

evals.prompt: Review my EBS setup in us-east-1 before our launch next week. Is my storage production-ready?
evals.expected_output: The agent runs Review mode and returns a rated report with the six areas: capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture and deletion protection. Each finding has a severity and a proposed fix. Areas it could not check are reported as gaps, not as healthy.
assertions: The response is the full rated report, not a summary or an offer to produce one.
Each finding has a severity of High, Medium, Low or Indeterminate.
Checks that could not be run are reported as gaps, not as passing.

assertions.text: No mutating call is reported as executed

evals.prompt: I was trying to create an io2 volume with 150K IOPS and got this error: You have exceeded your maximum io2 IOPS limit of 100000 IOPS in this region. What should I do?
evals.expected_output: The agent explains that the regional io2 IOPS quota, not the per-volume maximum, blocked the request. It reads the applied quota from Service Quotas, counts existing io2 IOPS usage, checks other Amazon EBS quotas against usage, and pre-fills a Service Quotas increase request as a proposal.
assertions: The response says the regional io2 IOPS quota, not the per-volume maximum, blocked the request.
The response reports current io2 IOPS usage against the applied quota.
The quota increase is proposed and not submitted without operator approval.
The quota recommendation includes intake questions for the customer to answer and a caution that the increase is not guaranteed and is decided by AWS.

evals.prompt: I tried to modify my EBS volume and it failed. ModifyVolume on my 15 GiB io2 volume returned 'Iops to volume size ratio of 1333.3 is too high; maximum is 1000' when I raised the IOPS to 20,000. Why did this EBS volume modification fail and what should I do?
evals.expected_output: The agent explains that io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB, so 20,000 IOPS needs at least 20 GiB, and proposes the size and IOPS change together as a directed action for operator approval.
assertions: The response explains the io2 limit of 1,000 IOPS per GiB.
The change is proposed for operator approval rather than run.

assertions.text: The minimum size of 20 GiB is stated

assertions: The response gives the exact parameters of the proposed change.
A typed approval in chat is not treated as approval to run the change.
